newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: France sets EU spinning over budget pact.
newsitem.headline: France sets EU spinning over budget pact.

text.p: France threw the European Union into turmoil on Monday, telling its partners it wanted time to study an already agreed deal designed to keep budget deficits from ballooning after the single currency is introduced.
Within moments of the news, financial markets reacted sharply with the French stock market and the franc falling against the German mark.
Officials insisted there was no question of reopening the hard-fought agreement and that it was a matter of allowing the new government time to look at it.
"The markets had expected a deal by Amsterdam. Now they will have to wait a bit," a source close to the German delegation said.
New French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn told his counterparts Paris wanted time to consider the plan, agreed in Dublin in December, but not yet ratified.
Paris would need at least a week, he said, adding that that meant he did not believe it could be done by the EU's summit on June 16 and 17 in Amsterdam.
Once EU source said Strauss-Kahn has said the government wanted to talk to the National Assembly and that that could not happen before June 19.
Strauss-Kahn said he did not want to renegotiate the pact. Other EU ministers and officials were quick to say the pact could not be reopened.
"What has been agreed upon and discussed for two years can no longer be put up for negotiation," German Finance Minister Theo Waigel told reporters.
European Monetary Affairs Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy said the request for parliament discussion did not threaten the launch date of January 1, 1999 for economic and monetary union (EMU).
Commission President Jacques Santer said he still hoped for a deal by Amsterdam but that the new French government's desire to discuss the issue was "understandable."

Dutch Finance Minister Gerrit Zalm, representing the EU presidency, said he also hoped for a deal by Amsterdam but acknowledged it could take time to integrate France's demand for a greater coordination of economic policies.
